lead: A model that memorises its training data can still fail on tomorrow's data. Generalisation is the ability to do well on data the model has not seen. The gap between training error and test error tells you whether a model is too simple or too flexible. The errors split into bias, variance and noise, and validation plus cross-validation expose overfitting before you deploy a model. The same ideas decide how many hidden units to use in a network or how many features to keep in a loan-approval model.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 on supervised learning, where a model fits a map from inputs to given labels.

sections.h3: Training error, test error and generalisation

blocks.text: Training error is the average loss on the examples used to fit the model. Test error is the average loss on fresh examples from the same problem. Generalisation is good performance on those fresh examples. A model that predicts well on unseen inputs has generalised; a model that only predicts its training labels has not.

Overfitting means low training error and high test error. The model has learned quirks of the training set, including noise. Underfitting means high training error and high test error. The model is too simple to capture the real pattern, so it misses on both sets.

Model complexity changes this balance. For a polynomial, complexity is the degree. For a neural network, complexity can be the number of hidden units or layers. As complexity rises, training error usually falls. Test error first falls, reaches a minimum, then rises. The minimum is the useful operating point for that data size.
High bias and high variance are the two failure modes behind these curves. A high-bias model underfits. A high-variance model overfits. The next section writes this split as a formula.

At one input x, let f(x) be the true target value and let ŷ(x) be the model's prediction. Train the model on many independent training sets of the same size. Average the squared error over those repeated runs. The expected squared error at x splits as follows.

blocks.where: E[·] is the average over repeated training sets; f(x) is the true target or conditional mean; ŷ(x) is the prediction; bias(x) = E[ŷ(x)] − f(x); bias²(x) is [bias(x)]²; variance(x) = E[(ŷ(x) − E[ŷ(x)])²]; σ² is the variance of the noise in the target.

blocks.text: Bias measures how far the average prediction is from the truth. Variance measures how much the prediction moves when the training set changes. σ² is irreducible noise: no model can remove it. A high-bias model is too rigid; a high-variance model is too sensitive to the sample.
Increasing complexity usually lowers bias² and raises variance. The best complexity balances the two. The expected test error can never go below σ².

Validation data is not used to fit weights. It is used to choose complexity or hyperparameters. A validation set gives an honest estimate during tuning. If you tune on the test set, the final test error is optimistic.
k-fold cross-validation uses all data for validation once. Use k = 5 or k = 10.

items: Split it into k equal folds.
For each fold i, train on the other k − 1 folds and validate on fold i.
Record the k validation errors and average them.
Choose the model with the lowest average; then retrain on all data and report once on a held-out test set.

blocks.text: Cross-validation matters when data is scarce. A single split can be lucky or unlucky. Averaging k runs reduces that luck. For time-series data, keep the time order and never let future data leak into the past.
Regularisation, dropout and early stopping reduce overfitting. They are the cures taught in Unit 2. Here, the diagnostic is the gap between training and validation error.

spec.title: Each row: bias², variance, σ², test MSE
spec.aria: A table of the worked example: for polynomial degrees 1, 3 and 9 the test MSE is split into bias squared, variance and noise variance 0.05, giving totals 0.48, 0.15 and 2.30, with high bias at degree 1, high variance at degree 9 and the lowest test error at degree 3.

examples.question: You fit polynomials of degree 1, 3 and 9 to 40 training points and test on 200 fresh points. The noise variance is σ² = 0.05. The test mean squared errors (MSE) are 0.48, 0.15 and 2.30. Repeated-training variance estimates are 0.03, 0.02 and 2.25. Training MSEs are 0.40, 0.13 and 0.001. (a) Compute bias² for each degree using test MSE = bias² + variance + σ². (b) State which degree underfits and which overfits.
steps: Write the decomposition for each degree: test MSE = bias² + variance + σ².
Degree 1: bias² = 0.48 − 0.03 − 0.05 = 0.40. Check: 0.40 + 0.03 + 0.05 = 0.48. Training MSE 0.40 and test MSE 0.48 are both high relative to σ² = 0.05, so this is high bias and underfitting.
Degree 3: bias² = 0.15 − 0.02 − 0.05 = 0.08. Check: 0.08 + 0.02 + 0.05 = 0.15. Training MSE 0.13 and test MSE 0.15 are close, so this is the balanced fit among the three.
Degree 9: bias² = 2.30 − 2.25 − 0.05 = 0.00. Check: 0.00 + 2.25 + 0.05 = 2.30. Training MSE 0.001 is tiny but test MSE 2.30 is large, so this is high variance and overfitting.
Compare the three fits: degree 1 has the highest bias², degree 9 has the highest variance, and degree 3 has the lowest test MSE.
examples.answer: Bias² values are 0.40, 0.08 and 0.00 in squared target units; degree 1 underfits with high bias and degree 9 overfits with high variance.
examples.check:
sigma2 = 0.05
test_mse = [0.48, 0.15, 2.30]
variance = [0.03, 0.02, 2.25]
for t, v in zip(test_mse, variance):
    bias2 = t - v - sigma2
    print(f"{bias2:.2f}")
    print(f"{bias2 + v + sigma2:.2f}")

traps: Judging a model by training error alone: a degree-9 polynomial can have training MSE 0.001 and test MSE 2.30.
Using the test set to choose the model, then reporting the same number as the final test error. Tune on validation or cross-validation; touch the test set once.
Expecting test error to reach zero: σ² is the expected noise floor, so no model can push the expected error below it.
Mixing up bias and variance: high bias means both training and test error are high; high variance means training error is low but test error is high.
Confusing model complexity with the number of training examples; adding data can reduce variance but does not remove bias.

quiz.q: Define training error and test error.
quiz.a: Training error is the average loss on the examples used to fit the model. Test error is the average loss on fresh unseen examples.

quiz.q: Why can a model with very low training error still be bad?
quiz.a: It may have memorised noise and quirks of the training set, giving high test error. Low training error alone does not show generalisation.

quiz.q: A model has test MSE 0.62, variance 0.20 and σ² = 0.07. Compute bias².
In 5-fold cross-validation, why average the five validation errors instead of trusting one fold?
quiz.a: Each fold is a small sample; one fold may be easy or hard. The average reduces split luck and gives a more stable estimate of generalisation.

quiz.q: Write the bias-variance decomposition for expected squared error at x and define each term.
quiz.a: E[(ŷ(x) − f(x))²] = bias²(x) + variance(x) + σ². bias(x) = E[ŷ(x)] − f(x); variance(x) = E[(ŷ(x) − E[ŷ(x)])²]; σ² is target noise variance.

quiz.q: Model A has training MSE 0.10 and test MSE 0.90. Model B has training MSE 0.50 and test MSE 0.55. σ² = 0.05. Which likely overfits and which underfits?
quiz.a: A likely overfits: low training error and high test error. B likely underfits: both errors are high relative to σ² = 0.05.

quiz.q: You add hidden units. Training error falls but validation error rises. What is happening and what should you do?
quiz.a: Variance is rising; the network is overfitting. Stop increasing complexity, use regularisation, dropout or early stopping, or add more data.

quiz.q: Why are k = 5 or k = 10 common choices in k-fold cross-validation?
quiz.a: They balance estimate stability and compute cost: 5 or 10 training runs are usually affordable, and each training set is 80% or 90% of the data.

beyond: Not for the exam. Very wide networks can show double descent: test error rises, then falls again as width grows past the interpolation point; only a few universities teach this curve. In industry, validation curves and cross-validation decide model release, and monitoring detects data drift after deployment. Search next for double descent, learning curves, and nested cross-validation.
